Summary

Countries are grouped into tiers by the IO data available for them, from the most detailed and annually updated (Tier 0) to countries with no usable published table (Tier 3).



Figure 1:Countries by tier. Darker means more detailed IO data. Small countries are shown as dots. Countries in gray are not modeled separately; they are part of the rest-of-world region.

The model covers 148 countries plus a rest-of-world region. A country’s tier sets which type of table it starts from, how much sector detail that table has, and how it is valued.

Country tier

Countries

Tier 0

United States

redefinitions, following BEA’s 2017 detailed schema

Tier 1

Tier 3

83 countries

No usable table: a template built from other countries’ tables

The U.S. starts from Make and Use tables for 2024 that Cornerstone produces each year (nowcasted tables). They follow the schema of the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) 2017 detailed tables, after redefinitions. BEA’s own detailed tables come out only every five years, and the latest are for 2017; our tables estimate the 2024 economy in the same form. In additional to Make and Use tables, we also estimate the Import Matrix, which defines the import proportion of each cell in the Use table.

Why after redefinitions? Many establishments make secondary products. A hotel runs a restaurant, for example, or a manufacturer does its own repair work. Redefinitions move these secondary products, and the inputs used to make them, to the industry where they are the primary product. Each industry’s input recipe then describes the product it is named for more closely, which makes for cleaner emission factors.

The U.S. tables have 405 sectors. The U.S. tables matter beyond the U.S.: their detailed structure sets the model’s common sector list, and it is used to split other countries’ coarser sectors (see 

ABSR).

All four are symmetric IO tables, with the same sectors on rows and columns. Each one is prepared the same way:

Map to the common sectors. A correspondence links each national sector to one or more of the 405 common sectors. Where one national sector covers several common sectors, it is split using the U.S. structure as weights (

structural reflection).

Split domestic and imported inputs using the country’s own domestic and import shares.

Convert to 2024 U.S. dollars. Values are converted at the data year’s average exchange rate, then brought to 2024 prices with a U.S. price index.

Keep the country’s total output. Total output by sector is anchored to the source table’s gross output.

Most of the remaining large economies come from one of two multi-regional tables, FIGARO or ICIO. Both are already harmonized across countries, but they are much coarser than the U.S. tables. Where a country is in both, we use FIGARO.

FIGARO countries: the 27 EU member states, plus Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Norway, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Switzerland, and Türkiye.

ICIO countries: Cambodia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Hong Kong, Iceland, Israel, Kazakhstan, Laos, Malaysia, Morocco, Myanmar, New Zealand, Peru, the Philippines, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand, Tunisia, and Viet Nam.

Both are inter-country tables, so each country’s own block of the table gives its domestic inputs, and the blocks for all other countries give its imports.

Before mapping, five of FIGARO’s broad sectors are split into finer ones while keeping their totals: electricity, gas, and heat; water, sewerage, and waste; basic metals (steel, other ferrous, non-ferrous); non-metallic minerals (cement, other); mining (five sectors); and agriculture (11 farm sectors). The tables are then mapped to the common sectors with 

ABSR, and converted to 2024 U.S. dollars the same way as Tier 1.

The 83 countries that are in neither Tier 1 nor Tier 2 have no usable published table. They are not part of the multi-region table; their factors are calculated one country at a time.

Input recipe. All 83 share one template recipe, a weighted blend of three Tier 2 economies: Mexico (30%), Malaysia (30%), and Tunisia (40%).

Imports. Each country’s own import share splits the template into domestic and imported inputs, with the same share for every sector. The supply chains behind those imports are approximated with China’s.

Emissions. Direct emission intensities are scaled to the country’s own emissions per unit of GDP, and electricity uses the country’s own emission intensity.

This template is separate from the rest-of-world region in the multi-region table, which is built from different countries (see 

The IO model: overview).

All tables are converted to 2024 U.S. dollars. Sector lists are reconciled in the later steps: mapping to the common sector list, linking with trade data, and balancing.

Key assumptions

Price basis does not change input recipes

Assumption: Countries publish their tables on different price bases (basic, producer, or purchaser prices, and sometimes a mix within one table). We use each table as published and assume these differences do not materially change the direct requirements (A).

Why we make it: Converting every table to one price basis needs product-level tax, subsidy, and margin data for each country, which is not consistently available.

How it affects results: Where product taxes or trade and transport margins are large, as for fuels, input coefficients could differ from those on a common price basis. See 

How-to 2: Purchaser vs. producer price, and margins.

U.S. margins for purchaser prices

Assumption: Factors are converted from producer to purchaser prices using U.S. trade and transport margins for every country.

Why we make it: Margin data comparable to the U.S. tables are not available for every country.

How it affects results: Where a country’s wholesale, retail, or transport margins differ from U.S. margins, its purchaser-price factors could be too high or too low. Producer-price factors are not affected. See 

How-to 2: Purchaser vs. producer price, and margins.

Tier 3 countries share one recipe

Assumption: Tier 3 countries share one template input recipe. Each country differs only in its overall import share, applied equally to every sector, and in its direct emission intensities, which are scaled to the country’s emissions per unit of GDP, with its own electricity intensity. Their imported supply chains are approximated with China’s.

Why we make it: These countries have no usable published IO table.

How it affects results: Differences in industry structure between Tier 3 countries are not captured, and imports from countries other than China are given China’s supply chains. Factors for these countries carry more uncertainty than those for Tiers 0 to 2.

Summary

Cornerstone uses standardized national input-output tables to represent production recipes and link them with global trade data, thus representing domestic and international supply chains.

Every country enters the model as a national IO table, but countries don’t all start from the same kind of table. The first step is to collect the best available table for each country and record where it came from: the source, version, year, valuation, and sector detail. Which table we start from depends on the country’s 

tier: the U.S. starts from 

Make and Use tables for 2024 that Cornerstone produces using BEA’s methodology, after 

redefinitions and following BEA’s 2017 detailed schema, while other countries start from national statistical agency tables, 

FIGARO or 

ICIO, or a template. See 

Country tiers for what each tier starts from.

The detailed U.S. structure sets the model’s common sector list, and it is used to split other countries’ coarser sectors (see 

ABSR). Sector lists and currencies are reconciled in the later steps: mapping to the common sector list, linking with trade data, and balancing.

Figure 1:The Supply and Use tables. Supply shows who makes each commodity; Use shows who buys it and what each industry adds in value. The Make table (*) is a variant of Supply that leaves imports to the Use table.

An economy’s IO accounts come as a pair of tables.

Supply (V) records the production of each commodity by each domestic industry, plus imports of each commodity. The Make table, used for the U.S., is a variant: it has the same production block but no imports row. Imports appear instead in the Use table’s final demand, as a negative column. Either way, the production block gives two output totals:

Industry output x: the sum across an industry’s row, which is everything the industry makes, including secondary products.

Commodity output q: the sum down a commodity’s column, which is everything domestic industries make of that commodity. Adding imports gives the total supply of the commodity.

Use (U and y) records who buys each commodity:

Intermediate use (U): the commodities each industry buys as inputs.

Final demand (y): the commodities bought by final users, namely households, government, investment, and exports.

Value added: below each industry’s inputs, its wages, taxes on production, and profits.

The two tables balance. For each commodity, total supply equals total use. For each industry, inputs plus value added equal the industry’s output x.

Figure 2:The Use table is split into domestic and imported use, for industries and final users alike.

A purchase can come from a domestic producer or from abroad, and the two lead to different supply chains. So the Use table is split in two:

Domestic use (Udom, ydom): commodities bought from domestic producers.

Imported use (Uimp, yimp): commodities bought from producers in other countries.

U = Udom + Uimp. Final demand splits the same way, with exports on the domestic side: y = ydom + exports + yimp. Imported use is later traced back to the countries that made the imports, using trade data. How each country’s tables arrive at this split is described in 

Country tiers.

Figure 3:Domestic and imported direct requirements are built from the same two steps.

The direct requirements tables turn the Supply and Use tables into recipes: the inputs needed to make $1 of each commodity. They take three steps.

Inputs per dollar of industry output. Divide each industry’s column of domestic use by its output x.

Market shares. Divide each commodity’s column of the Supply table by its output q. This gives the share of each commodity made by each industry.

Combine. Multiply the two to get inputs per dollar of each commodity. Doing this with domestic use gives Adom; doing it with imported use gives Aimp.

For more details on the math behind it, contact 

team@cornerstonedata​.org.

Adom and Aimp add up to the total direct requirements A. A column of A is the input recipe for $1 of that commodity, split by where the inputs come from.

Tables that are already symmetric, with the same sectors on rows and columns, skip step 2: their domestic and imported use are divided by output directly. This applies to the Tier 1 and Tier 2 tables.

hierarchy.lvl2: Final demand for the national accounting balance
Final demand for the national accounting balance

records.content:
Final demand in the Use table includes purchases of imports. To match domestic production, we need final demand for domestic products only. We call this ynab, the final demand for the national accounting balance: domestic final demand for domestic products (ydom) plus exports.

Here ydom is what households, government, and investment buy from domestic producers, and yimp is what they buy from abroad. Imports not bought by industries go to final users, so yimp is total imports less the row sums of Uimp. Exports are the country’s own production, so they count toward ynab in full.

With ynab, the model reproduces the country’s commodity output: running ynab through the domestic supply chain (the Leontief inverse of Adom) gives back q. This is a check that the tables, Adom, and ynab are consistent.

hierarchy.lvl2: From single-country tables to the multi-region model
From single-country tables to the multi-region model

records.content:
Figure 4:The 

MRIO direct requirements table. Each country’s domestic inputs sit on the diagonal; its imported inputs are spread down its column by country of origin.

Each country’s tables say how much of its inputs are imported, but not where they come from. The multi-region model links the countries so that a supply chain can be followed across borders.

Put every country in one table. The 65 countries in Tiers 0 to 2 each get their own block, so A is a 65 × 65 grid of country blocks, each 405 × 405 sectors. Each country’s Adom sits on the diagonal. A country’s column holds everything its industries buy; the rows say which country sold it.

Split imports by origin. Each country’s Aimp is spread down its column using bilateral trade data (

BACI): for each product, the share the country imports from each origin. Products the trade data don’t cover, mostly services, use origin shares from 

FIGARO or 

ICIO. Imported final demand (yimp) is split the same way.

Add the rest of the world. Imports from countries outside the table come from a rest-of-world region. Its domestic input structure is pooled from the tables of Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile. It is added as one more block, making A a 66 × 66 grid of country blocks. This region is separate from the template used for Tier 3 countries’ own factors (see 

Country tiers).

Balance. The table is balanced with 

RAS, so that each country’s sales to all users, at home and abroad, add up to its output, without changing it’s domestic recipe. This makes small adjustments to the import coefficients.

Solve. The total requirements (L) are calculated for the whole table at once, so supply chains that cross several borders are captured in full (see 

below).

The other 83 of the model’s 148 countries (Tier 3) are linked to this table more simply; see 

Country tiers.

A shows only a sector’s direct suppliers. Take $1 of furniture. Its column of A lists what the furniture maker buys to make it: lumber, hardware, electricity, transport. These are the first tier of the supply chain.

Each of those suppliers has its own column in A. The sawmill buys logs, fuel, and machinery; the power plant buys fuel and equipment. These purchases are the second tier. Each supplier’s column is scaled by how much of it the first tier needs: if the furniture maker buys 20 cents of lumber for each $1 of furniture, the sawmill’s whole recipe is multiplied by 0.20. The second-tier suppliers have their own suppliers, the third tier, scaled again by what the second tier needs, and so on, without end. In the multi-region model the trace crosses borders: a second-tier supplier may be a steel mill in another country.

Each tier is smaller than the one before, because every dollar of output pays for value added (wages, taxes, profits) as well as purchases. So the tiers add up to a finite total: everything produced, anywhere in the supply chain, to deliver $1 of each commodity to a final user. Written out, that total is I + A + A² + A³ + …, where I is the $1 of the commodity itself, A the first tier, A² the second, and so on.

There is a simple way to calculate this infinite sum all at once: a special inverse of A, (I − A)⁻¹, called the Leontief inverse after the economist Wassily Leontief. That is why the result is called L. A column of L shows the total output needed from every sector, in every country, for $1 of final demand for that commodity.

Note

The tiers here are rounds of suppliers in a supply chain. They are not the same as the 

country tiers, which describe the data available for each country.

hierarchy.lvl3: What the model can and can’t trace
What the model can and can’t trace

records.content:
L follows supply chains through the 66 countries in the multi-region table. The 83 Tier 3 countries are not separate parts of that table, so supply chains can’t be traced to them one by one.

Question

Can the model answer it?

How much of a U.S. product’s supply chain is in China, Germany, or Korea?

Yes. Each of the 65 countries has its own part of the table.

How much is in Kenya or Egypt specifically?

No. Imports from all Tier 3 countries are grouped into the rest-of-world region.

Do the emissions traced to the rest of the world reflect those countries?

Not directly. The region’s input recipe and emission intensities come from Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile.

Where do a Tier 3 country’s own supply chains lead?

Only to its own economy and to its imports as a whole, which are approximated with China’s supply chains.

Key assumptions

Industry technology

Assumption: An industry uses the same input recipe for everything it makes, its primary product and any secondary products alike. This is what lets the market shares (V ÷ q) turn industry recipes into commodity recipes.

Why we make it: It is the standard assumption for building commodity-by-commodity tables from Supply and Use tables, and unlike the alternative (commodity technology) it never produces negative requirements.

How it affects results: A secondary product takes on its producer’s recipe. Using U.S. tables after 

redefinitions keeps secondary products, and so this effect, small.

Import proportionality

Assumption: Within a country, every buyer of a product gets the same mix of origins. If a country imports 30% of its steel from Korea, every industry that buys imported steel gets 30% of it from Korea.

Why we make it: Trade data record which countries trade each product, but not which industry buys the imports.

How it affects results: An industry that in reality buys mostly from one origin gets the national average mix instead. Where origins differ a lot in emission intensity, this can move that industry’s factors.

The rest of the world looks like four proxy economies

Assumption: The rest-of-world region stands in for every country outside the multi-region table, including all Tier 3 countries, as a source of imports. Its input recipe and emission intensities are pooled from Colombia, Mexico, Türkiye, and Chile. It buys nothing from other regions, so a supply chain that reaches it stays there.

Why we make it: Countries outside the table have no linked IO tables of their own, and these four are the lower-income OECD economies in the table.

How it affects results: Imports from Tier 3 countries carry the proxy economies’ emission intensities rather than their own. Supply chains can’t be traced to individual Tier 3 countries, or onward from the rest of the world to other regions.

Data-year recipes, shares, and intensities still apply in 2024

Assumption: The IO tables, emissions, trade shares, and gap-fill shares come from different years (for example, 2024 trade data with IO tables and emissions from 2018 to 2023). We assume the input recipes, origin shares, and emission intensities from each source’s data year still describe the 2024 economy. Each country’s emissions are divided by its output from the same year; that output is re-priced to 2024 dollars with a U.S. price index, so its direct emission intensities are data-year intensities per 2024 dollar.

Why we make it: National tables, multi-regional databases, and trade data are published on different schedules, and we use the most recent of each.

How it affects results: Where an economy’s structure, trading partners, or emission intensity changed between the data year and 2024 (for example, a cleaner electricity grid), the model reflects the earlier pattern. Using one U.S. price index for every country means price changes elsewhere are not captured. The years used for each country are listed in

Starter definitions drawn from the site plan; team to review and extend. Terms defined here can be linked from any page with {term}`MRIO` and show a hover definition.

ABSR

Auto-Balanced Structural Reflection. The method that expands a country’s coarser IO table onto the model’s common sector schema, using U.S. structure as weights, while keeping the country’s accounts balanced.

Basic price

The amount a producer receives for a product, excluding taxes on products and including subsidies on products.

BACI

The CEPII database of bilateral international trade by product, used to split each country’s imports by country of origin.

Country tier

A group of countries modeled with the same level of detail and the same kinds of data sources: Tier 0, detailed annual IO tables (the United States); Tier 1, detailed periodic national IO tables; Tier 2, coarse multi-regional tables from FIGARO or ICIO; and Tier 3, no IO tables (a template built from other countries).

EEIO

Environmentally-extended input-output model. An input-output model of an economy with environmental data (here, greenhouse gas emissions) attached to each sector.

FIGARO

Full International and Global Accounts for Research in input-Output analysis. Multi-regional IO tables from Eurostat and the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre, used for many Tier 2 countries.

GWP

Global warming potential. The warming effect of 1 kg of a gas relative to 1 kg of CO₂ over a time horizon. The model uses AR6 values with a 100-year horizon.

Make/Use framework

IO tables that record which industries make which commodities (Make, or supply) and which commodities each industry and final user buys (Use).

Margins

The trade and transport costs added between the producer and the buyer: transport, wholesale, and retail.

MRIO

Multi-regional input-output model. Country IO tables linked into one global system through international trade.

ICIO

The OECD Inter-Country Input-Output tables, used for Tier 2 countries not covered by FIGARO.

Producer price

The basic price plus taxes on products, less subsidies on products, excluding margins.

Purchaser price

The price the buyer pays: the producer price plus trade and transport margins. The published factors are per dollar of purchaser price.

RAS

An iterative method that scales the rows and columns of a table until it matches known row and column totals.

Redefinitions

Adjustments that move secondary products (and their inputs) to the industry where they are the primary product.

Structural reflection

Using a detailed table’s structure (here, the U.S. tables) as weights to split a coarser table into finer sectors.
